title: Sikkim Tunnel Death Toll Rises to Ten as Rescuers Battle Gas and Debris
excerpt: Ten bodies recovered from the collapsed ADIT-3 tunnel at NHPC's Teesta Stage VI hydroelectric project in Namchi district, with more than 15 workers still feared trapped inside the gas-filled passage.
body:
• Ten workers confirmed dead after a suspected gas blast collapsed an under-construction hydroelectric tunnel in Sikkim's Namchi district on Monday; the toll rose from seven overnight
  • At least 25 people — workers and project officials — were inside the ADIT-3 tunnel when the explosion occurred; more than 15 remain trapped, and officials warn survival chances are slim
  • Recovered bodies are charred, pointing to a powerful methane or natural gas explosion rather than a simple landslide, according to state disaster management officials
  • Prime Minister Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah have assured full central support; NDRF, SDRF, police, and fire teams are on site using gas masks and oxygen cylinders

Blast and Collapse Sequence

A suspected gas explosion ripped through an under-construction tunnel in Sikkim's Namchi district on Monday, triggering a landslide that sealed the entrance and trapped at least 25 workers and project officials inside. By Tuesday morning, the confirmed death toll had risen to ten — up from seven reported overnight — with authorities warning the number could climb further as rescue teams push deeper into the debris-choked passage.

https://x.com/ani_digital/status/2079447089684353337

The disaster struck the ADIT-3 tunnel of NHPC's Teesta Stage VI Hydroelectric Project in Samardung village, Jholungey. Workers were inside the tunnel during active construction when the blast occurred, sending rock and earth crashing across the entrance and cutting off those deeper inside.

"The incident was caused by a possible natural gas blast but we cannot say for sure yet. Nine bodies have been recovered — the bodies are charred, so it suggests there was a blast."

— Rajiv Roka, Sikkim State Disaster Management Official

A tenth body was recovered by 9:30 a.m. on Tuesday, according to a statement from Namchi police. Of the seven victims identified so far, four hailed from West Bengal's Jalpaiguri district, while the others came from Assam, Punjab, Uttarakhand's Dehradun, and Namchi itself. Three bodies remain unidentified and have been sent to District Hospital Singtam and STNM Hospital.

Toxic Gas Hampers Rescue

Rescue operations, launched within hours of the collapse, have been severely complicated by a suspected gas leak inside the tunnel. It remains unclear whether the gas — believed to be methane — leaked from a pipeline or emanated from rock formations disturbed by the blast.

Multiple rescuers reported difficulty breathing upon entering the tunnel, and several lost consciousness, forcing teams from the National Disaster Response Force, State Disaster Response Force, police, and the fire department to adopt a cautious, phased approach. Responders wore gas masks and carried oxygen cylinders as they worked their way through the passage.

Sixteen workers have been pulled out alive and taken to the primary health centre in Rangpo for medical examination, according to state government statements. But state disaster management official Rajiv Roka warned Reuters that survival chances for the remaining trapped workers were slim, given the gas concentration and structural instability inside the tunnel.

Central Government Responds

The disaster has drawn swift responses from New Delhi. Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke with Sikkim Chief Minister Prem Singh Tamang, expressing deep concern and assuring full central assistance. Union Home Minister Amit Shah also called Tamang to take stock of rescue operations.

"My heartfelt condolences go to the families of the workers who have lost their lives. In this hour of grief, the thoughts and prayers of the entire state are with the bereaved families, and we stand firmly by them during this difficult time."

— Prem Singh Tamang, Chief Minister of Sikkim

NHPC, the state-owned power company operating the project, did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Reuters. The Teesta Stage VI project is one of several hydroelectric installations on the Teesta river — a waterway that has been central to Sikkim's development ambitions and its recurring disasters.

Pattern of Himalayan Construction Disasters

The tunnel collapse adds to a grim pattern of construction-related fatalities in India's Himalayan infrastructure push. In 2023, 41 workers were trapped for 17 days inside a collapsed tunnel in Uttarakhand's Silkyara, an incident that exposed systemic safety gaps in high-altitude construction. In October 2023, a glacial lake breach and flash floods devastated Sikkim's Teesta valley, destroying the Teesta Stage III dam at Chungthang and killing over a dozen people.

Environmental groups and geologists have repeatedly warned that large-scale tunnelling and dam construction in the seismically active, geologically fragile Himalayas heightens the risk of catastrophic failures — especially during the monsoon season, when saturated rock is more prone to collapse.

Impact on Diaspora Communities

For the Indian diaspora, particularly those with roots in northeastern India and the migrant-worker communities of West Bengal, Assam, and Uttarakhand, the disaster is a reminder of the human cost borne by workers who build the country's infrastructure in its most hazardous terrain. The victims' home states — Jalpaiguri, Dehradun, Punjab, Assam — reflect the migrant labour networks that power India's construction sector.

Rescue teams continue to work through the night. Authorities have urged families gathered at the site to remain patient as crews work to ventilate the tunnel and locate the remaining trapped workers.
